newsitem.title: CHINA: FEATURE - Female smiles and male minds power China airline.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Female smiles and male minds power China airline.

text.p: For Chen Feng, chairman and president of the Chinese regional carrier Hainan Airlines, a woman's place is on board -- and not in the boardroom.

Attractive young air hostesses were an essential part of the superior in-flight service needed to help to power Hainan Airlines through the turbulent skies of China's fast-growing and fiercely competitive aviation sector, Chen said.

But no women sat on the board of the youthful company, which plans to fund a major fleet expansion with China's first public airline share issue, he said in an interview at his headquarters in Haikou, capital of the southern island province of Hainan.

"If ladies too beautiful are too close to me...I will forget my work," said 45-year-old Chen, who calls himself the old man of Hainan Airlines' management and says the relative youth of many of his fellow staff gives him extra clout to steer the firm.
"We can use young men...and I have bigger power," he said, adding that younger managers were harder working, more flexible and bolder.

Company officials say management agility has been a major advantage for their airline, which built a 1989 government start-up loan of just 10 million yuan ($1.2 million) into total assets of 1.954 billion yuan by 1995.

The company became China's first shareholding airline in 1992, a move that allowed it to begin accumulating its mostly-leased fleet of nine Boeing Corp 737s and a handful of turboprops and executive jets.
In 1995, it sold a 25 percent stake to American Aviation Investment, a fund partly controlled by U.S. financier George Soros, making it China's first joint-venture airline.
LOANS, BONDS, SHARES AND AIRLINERS

Hainan's ambitious purchasing plans have not always come to fruition, but Chen said the company was determined to buy four Boeing 737-400 airliners, three new-generation 737-800s with options on a further three, and three 767s.

Bank loans, overseas bonds and a public airline share issue would be used to muster the $600 million needed to acquire the Boeings along with seven new Metro 23 turboprops from U.S. manufacturer Fairchild Aircraft Inc, he said.
Hainan expected to be ready by the end of March to raise at least $30 million by issuing 80 million foreign currency 'B' shares and two million yuan-denominated 'A' shares, he said.
The shares are to be listed in Shanghai, making Hainan the first airline to list publicly on a domestic Chinese exchange.
Bonds worth around $300 million would also be issued in the United States, Chen said.

Company officials said rapid growth was the only option in China's competitive market, where state-owned regional carriers, margins narrowed by state controls on ticket pricing, joust for passengers on the more lucrative routes.
"We want to grow up...(there's) no other choice," said Chen. "If we are too small a big airline will take over us."

Germany's Lufthansa and Cathay Pacific of Hong Kong were worthy models for Hainan Airlines as it sought its own route to success through China's uncharted market, he said, adding that one U.S. carrier that used air hostesses of a certain age provided a negative example.
"It's very bad...not like young girls," he said. "That is not good service."
FOREIGN METHODS, CHINESE CULTURE

Modern foreign business techniques could only be successful in China if allied with an understanding of Chinese culture, said Chen, proudly showing guests the traditionally-styled study he keeps behind his Western-decorated office and boardroom.
The study, with its classical texts, ancient writing table and 270 kg (595 lb) metal dragon head, was a metaphor for a need to preserve the spirit of the nation, he said.
Cultural senstitivity was also vital for foreign companies, he said, adding that Boeing's success in China was largely due to its early arrival and sympathy for local customs.
Only Boeing had shown interest when Hainan began looking for its first airliners -- while the U.S. firm's European arch-rival Airbus Industrie had not even been in touch, he said.
"I love Airbus, but Airbus forgot me," he said.
Hainan Airlines' 1995 annual report showed revenues rose to 487.89 million yuan from 388.99 million yuan the year before. Officials said final 1996 figures were not yet available.
The 1995 report showed profits after tax as dipping to 81.20 million yuan from 87.16 million yuan in 1994, but Chen said profit growth had been continuous.
"Every year our revenues increase over 70 percent... Our profits have never fallen," he said but did not elaborate.

Company officials tout their freedom from the hidebound corporate culture of their competitors as the key to providing a level of service rare in China, where customer relations were largely neglected during decades of command-economy communism.
But chief economist Li Bing said even at Hainan Airlines training staff to international standards was no easy task.
"We are trying to persuade the air hostesses to smile," Li said. "It's very difficult."
